newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss banks to look out for dormant Nazi assets.
newsitem.headline: Swiss banks to look out for dormant Nazi assets.

text.p: Swiss banks, confronted with possible Nazi names in a huge list of Holocaust-era accounts, on Friday said safety checks built into the process of returning dormant wealth would stop war criminals from claiming cash.

But the Swiss Bankers' Association declined to say how much money there was in a handful of accounts that Jewish groups say might have been set up by Nazis. The banks have published the names of the registered holders of nearly 1,800 accounts holding a total of 61 million Swiss francs ($40 million).

"We are not providing details at the moment. We are investigating and we will see later whether we do something and what we do," Swiss Bankers' Association spokeswoman Silvia Matile told Reuters. "There are checks built in to prevent criminal money being paid out."
The bankers' association pledged to follow up on tips from Jewish organisations about suspected Nazi names and pass them to the Federal Banking Commission and the Swiss government.

The Nazi-hunting Simon Wiesenthal Centre in Los Angeles said the list of accounts included the names of at least eight prominent Nazis or collaborators. The accounts on the list were all opened by non-Swiss before the end of World War Two, most of whom have not been heard from since 1945.
The names raised the prospect of old Nazis or their heirs profiting from the efforts to restore lost wealth to Jews and others murdered or persecuted by the Nazis.
The restitution process was launched on Wednesday when the banks published the names of dormant account owners in newspapers worldwide and on the Internet (www.dormantaccounts.ch).
Owners or heirs were urged to approach any of five global contact offices and file claims that will be decided by an international Claims Resolution Panel of experienced arbitrators.

The process will be supervised by a three-member international board headed by former U.S. central bank governor Paul Volcker. Volcker also heads a mixed Jewish-Swiss commission probing Swiss bank vaults for further dormant accounts.
Matile said both the panel and Volcker's commission would also be checking that no ill-gotten money was paid out.
Matile said the Bankers' Association would provide the suspected Nazi names to Volcker and to the panel when it was established in the next few weeks.

The Wiesenthal centre faxed a first list of six names who might have been members of the Nazi elite to the Bankers' Association on Wednesday, shortly after the accounts list was published. It also found two that corresponded to infamous collaborators.
The six were Willy Bauer, Elisabeth Eder, Hermann Esser, Hermann Schmitz, Heinrich Hoffman and Karl Jager.

Bauer was an alias used by Anton Burger, an aide to mass murderer Adolf Eichmann and deputy commandant of the Theresienstadt concentration camp; Eder was the wife of Ernst Kaltenbrunner, the head of the SD, the Nazis' intelligence arm; Esser was vice president of the Reichstag parliament; Hoffmann was a Hitler confidant and Jager the head of Nazi intelligence in Lithuania.
The collaborators were Vojtech Tuka, the Nazi puppet premier of Slovakia who was executed in Bratislava in 1946 for war crimes, and Mercier Du Paty, the Marquis De Clam, a Vichy French official.

New York's World Jewish Congress also said several names on the list were troubling, including that of Dr Hans Wendland, who helped the Third Reich loot the art treasures of Europe. ($ = 1.510 Swiss Francs)
